abstracts.abstract: We introduce a novel framework for analyzing recursive algorithms based on differential dynamic logic, shifting the paradigm from traditional recurrence relation methods to a continuous-time verification approach. Unlike conventional techniques that rely on discrete summations and asymptotic approximations, our method models algorithm execution as hybrid dynamical systems where computational steps evolve continuously. We establish fundamental theorems connecting the operational semantics of recursive procedures to invariant conditions in the continuous domain. The framework enables precise characterization of algorithmic complexity without relying on implicit smoothness assumptions. We demonstrate its versatility by applying it to three distinct problem domains: divide-and-conquer algorithms, probabilistic recursive procedures, and self-adjusting data structures. Our analysis reveals previously unknown tight bounds for merge sort variants and provides constructive proofs of optimality for several classic recursive schemes. The proposed paradigm fundamentally reconceptualizes how we reason about algorithmic behavior, offering a unified perspective that subsumes traditional complexity analysis as a special case. This work opens new avenues for cross-pollination between formal methods and algorithm design, suggesting that the rigid boundary between verification and analysis is more permeable than previously understood.

We present significant improvements to the known complexity bounds for the synthesis of concurrent programs from temporal logic specifications. The state-of-the-art approaches based on alternating automata constructions exhibit doubly-exponential complexity in the size of the specification formula. By introducing a novel symbolic representation using ordered binary decision diagrams with parameterized partitioning, we reduce this to a single exponential blowup while preserving completeness guarantees. Our key technical contribution is a stratification theorem demonstrating that the determinization step can be avoided through careful encoding of the acceptance conditions. We prove that the synthesis problem for LTL on finite traces, which underlies most practical program synthesis scenarios, can now be solved in time O(2^n) where n depends only on the size of the environmental interface rather than the formula length. Experimental validation on established benchmark suites confirms that our approach yields orders-of-magnitude speedups in practice. The improved complexity has profound implications for scalability in industrial contexts, enabling synthesis for specifications that were previously beyond tractable analysis. We also provide matching lower bounds, establishing the optimality of our algorithm under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions.

We present VerdiNets, a new programming framework for specifying and verifying distributed protocols that fundamentally departs from existing refinement-based approaches. VerdiNets introduces the concept of executable network models where protocol correctness is guaranteed by construction through a novel type system that tracks causal dependencies and ordering constraints at the type level. Unlike traditional verification tools that employ offline model checking or interactive theorem proving, VerdiNets enables runtime verification with negligible overhead, catching protocol violations before they manifest as safety-critical failures. The framework supports a spectrum of fault models ranging from benign crash failures to Byzantine behavior, with consistent semantics across this spectrum. We have implemented VerdiNets as an extension to a functional programming language, providing developers with familiar abstraction mechanisms while guaranteeing compliance with specified fault-tolerance requirements. Case studies involving leader election, state machine replication, and consensus protocols demonstrate that VerdiNets can express complex real-world systems while maintaining provable correctness properties. The paradigm shift from post-hoc verification to constructively correct-by-construction systems represents a fundamental change in how we approach distributed software development.

We introduce GPHash, a high-performance concurrent hash table achieving throughput substantially exceeding current state-of-the-art implementations. GPHash combines fine-grained locking with lock-free read operations, carefully balancing contention reduction against memory consistency overhead. Our design addresses the fundamental tension between correctness under concurrent access and performance through a novel hierarchical locking scheme that adapts dynamically to access patterns. We present a comprehensive formal specification of the algorithm's behavior, proving linearizability for all operations through a reduction to a simpler sequential specification. The implementation includes adaptive resizing strategies that maintain load factor within optimal bounds without introducing unnecessary synchronization delays. Benchmarks on modern multi-socket architectures demonstrate up to 3.7x improvement in mixed read-write workloads compared to the best existing concurrent hash tables. GPHash handles extreme contention scenarios gracefully, maintaining predictable latency even under adversarial access patterns that cause pathological behavior in competing designs. The system is available as a library with language bindings for C, C++, and Rust, accompanied by extensive documentation and a property-based testing suite that has uncovered subtle bugs in previous implementations.
